summary:
We developed Echoes of Space, an interactive 3D web museum built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js that brings NASA’s abandoned hardware on the Moon and Mars to life. Users can freely rotate 3D globes of both celestial bodies, click on spacecraft placed at their exact NASA landing coordinates—including Apollo 11, Surveyor 3, Viking 1, Spirit, and Opportunity—inspect 3D models in 360 degrees, and read engaging first-person stories.
Our project directly addresses the challenge by turning dense technical mission archives into an intuitive, story-driven experience tailored for school-age space enthusiasts. Instead of reading dry tables, young learners connect with each machine’s journey and scientific discoveries. This matters because sharing these untold stories in an accessible, browser-based format sparks curiosity about space exploration and shows how yesterday’s pioneers paved the way for tomorrow’s missions.
details: Echoes of Space is an interactive 3D web museum built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js that brings NASA’s abandoned hardware on the Moon and Mars to life for school-age space enthusiasts. Using NASA Open Data, users can rotate 3D globes of the Moon and Mars, click on spacecraft placed at their exact landing coordinates—such as Apollo 11, Surveyor 3, Viking 1, Spirit, and Opportunity inspect their 360-degree 3D models, and read engaging first-person stories about their missions and scientific discoveries. By transforming dense technical archives into an accessible, browser-based visual experience without requiring any installation, our team aimed to balance scientific accuracy with clear, inspiring storytelling that sparks curiosity in space exploration and planetary science.
dataRefs: The NSSDCA is NASA's definitive, publicly available catalog. Participants can use it to search for any spacecraft or instrument sent into space, retrieve its mission parameters, and learn exactly what its final resting place and operational status is.

The descent stages of the Lunar Modules (like Apollo 11's Eagle) were left behind as launch pads.
https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1969-059C
Three electric "moon buggies" driven by astronauts. Parked permanently on the Moon.
https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1971-063C
Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Packages (seismometers, retroreflectors, etc.) left to do science after astronauts departed.
https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1969-099C
Robotic probes sent in the 1960s to prove soft landings were possible.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/surveyor-3/
The first rover on Mars (1997), delivered by the Pathfinder lander. Now permanently parked.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-pathfinder/
Twin rovers that operated for years. Both are now inactive monuments to Mars exploration.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-exploration-rovers-spirit-and-opportunity/
The first U.S. landers to successfully operate on Mars (1976), remaining exactly where they touched down.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/viking-1/
Phoenix dug for water ice; InSight listened for marsquakes. Both eventually lost power.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/insight/
Mapped Vesta and Ceres. Ran out of fuel and remains in a perpetual, unpowered orbit around Ceres.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/dawn/
First spacecraft to orbit and land on an asteroid. Left resting on the surface of 433 Eros.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/near-shoemaker/
Early deep-space probes that explored the outer planets. Now drifting silently out of the solar system.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/pioneer-10/
The first aircraft on another planet. Sustained rotor damage and became a stationary artifact.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-2020-perseverance/ingenuity-mars-helicopter/
Revolutionary exoplanet-hunting telescope that ran out of fuel and is drifting in an Earth-trailing orbit.
